Every provenance event in a federal supply chain can carry a signature from the party that made it.

GovChain records supply-chain provenance events as signed attestations. Each event, such as a lot received, an inspection passed or a handoff between suppliers, is signed by the party that made it, so a downstream buyer or auditor can verify the signature and the signer's identity without asking the source to confirm by email.

It runs on the same Ed25519 signing model as the AuthiChain protocol. Signed records support your own supply-chain risk management work; they are not a substitute for it, and they do not make anyone CMMC certified. Which controls apply to your contracts is something to evaluate with your contracting officer and assessor.

If you manage sub-tier suppliers and provenance still lives in spreadsheets, see what a signed chain of custody looks like.

https://govchain.us/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=govchain-part-provenance&utm_content=b

reddit.title: Has anyone tried signed attestations for sub-tier supplier provenance records?
reddit.body:
GovChain records provenance events (lot received, inspection passed, handoff between suppliers) as signed attestations, so each event carries a signature from the party that made it. A downstream buyer or auditor can verify the signature and the signer's identity without asking the source to confirm. It uses the same Ed25519 signing model as the rest of the AuthiChain protocol.

To be clear about scope: signed records are one input to supply-chain risk management. They don't make anyone CMMC certified, and which controls apply is a question for your contracting officer and assessor.

Curious how primes and subs here handle this today, and whether anyone has tried signed records instead of spreadsheets.
